rationale: 'Horace Mann is associated with' asks the test-taker to identify a historical development (the common-school/public-school reform movement). Mann's work belongs to the antebellum reform wave covered by 4.11 'An Age of Reform'.

The stem asks what rhetorical purpose Stowe's disclaimer served, i.e. to explain the author's purpose/audience strategy in the 1852 preface. The 1852 anti-slavery source fits the intensifying sectional conflict of the 1850s (5.6 'Failure of Compromise').

'Radical Republicans favored all of the following EXCEPT' asks the test-taker to identify positions of a historical group (military rule, Johnson impeachment, Black officeholding). Radical Reconstruction is 5.10 'Reconstruction'.

'The Dawes Act' asks the test-taker to identify what a federal policy did (individual allotments to break up tribal holdings). The Dawes Act is federal Indian policy within westward expansion's economic/land development (6.2).

'The best evidence that working-class living standards improved in this era comes from' asks which evidence best supports a claim (real wages vs. living costs), i.e. evaluating how evidence supports an argument. Working-class standards in the Gilded Age fall under 6.7 'Labor in the Gilded Age'.

The stem asks how Twain's 1900 anti-imperialism relates to an earlier American tradition (the republican fear that empire corrupts liberty), i.e. relating one development to another. The content is the post-1898 imperialism debate; FLAG: the item's period field says U6 but the content (Twain, Philippines, 1900) belongs to U7, so topic 7.2 'Imperialism: Debates' is the content-correct code.

'All of the following moved America toward war with Germany EXCEPT' asks the test-taker to identify the developments pushing the US toward WWI entry (unrestricted U-boats, Lusitania, Zimmermann Telegram). US entry into WWI is 7.5 'World War I: Military and Diplomacy'.

'In 1928, in most Eastern cities, one could find' asks the test-taker to identify a feature of 1920s urban life (the Prohibition-era speakeasy). 1920s cultural controversies including Prohibition are 7.8.

'The popularity of Huey Long and Father Coughlin showed that' asks the test-taker to identify the significance of a development (left-wing critics arguing the New Deal did too little). Critics of the New Deal fall under 7.10 'The New Deal'.

'The Battle of Midway proved decisive in the Pacific war because it' asks for the explanation of a development's significance (destruction of Japan's offensive carrier power), not mere identification. The Pacific war is 7.13 'World War II: Military'.

'Consumer spending rose in the 1950s because of all of the following EXCEPT' asks the test-taker to identify drivers of a development (postwar mass consumption: autos, homes, advertising). The postwar economy is 8.4 'Economy after 1945'.

'SDS membership was at its all-time high when' asks the test-taker to identify a development (the 1965-67 peak of student activism driven by Vietnam escalation/draft). The 1960s student movement is 8.12 'Youth Culture of the 1960s'.

'Ford's WIN program convinced many Americans that' asks the test-taker to identify the public meaning of a development (the 'Whip Inflation Now' gimmick as evidence Ford lacked an economic program). Ford/stagflation-era malaise falls under 8.14 'Society in Transition'.

The stem relates Greenspan's 1996 'irrational exuberance' warning to its outcome (the dot-com crash of 2000-2001), i.e. relating one development to a later one. The late-1990s economy is 9.4 'A Changing Economy'.

'The Obama foreign-policy initiative Trump vowed to overturn was' asks the test-taker to identify a development (the Iran nuclear deal/JCPOA reversal). Trump-era reversals of Obama policy fall under 9.6 'Challenges of the 21st Century'.
